solution.concept_anchor: Sikkim — protectorate status, not princely state under IoA
elimination_logic: Step 1: Is Assertion (A) correct? A states that Sikkim's integration into India did not use the Instrument of Accession framework. Sikkim was a protectorate (not a British paramountcy princely state) and its integration was achieved through the 36th Constitutional Amendment (1975) after a referendum. A is correct.

Step 2: Is Reason (R) correct? R states that Sikkim was a protectorate with a separate treaty relationship with India under the 1950 Treaty, distinct from the paramountcy relationship that governed princely states. This is factually accurate — Sikkim's relationship with India post-1947 was governed by the 1950 Indo-Sikkim Treaty, not the IoA framework. R is correct.

Step 3: Does R causally explain A? R explains why Sikkim's integration used a different mechanism — because it was a protectorate under a separate treaty, not a princely state under British paramountcy, so the IoA framework simply did not apply to it. R does causally explain A.
Both A and R correct, R explains A → correct option is (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap targets students who group Sikkim with other small princely states that acceded through the IoA. Sikkim's legal status was fundamentally different — it was never under British paramountcy in the same way as Indian princely states. The 1950 Indo-Sikkim Treaty established a protectorate relationship directly with independent India, bypassing the IoA framework entirely. Students who recall that 'Sikkim joined India in 1975' without knowing its prior legal status will conflate it with IoA-based accessions.
solution.final_explanation:
Sikkim's pathway to India is unique in constitutional history — it used a mechanism unavailable to any other territory.

**Assertion (A):** Correct. Sikkim was integrated through the 36th Constitutional Amendment (1975), which added it as the 22nd state. Article 2A was inserted (and later repealed after the provision became redundant). No Instrument of Accession was signed — the IoA framework was entirely inapplicable.

**Reason (R):** Correct. Sikkim was a protectorate, not a British paramountcy state. Its relationship with independent India was governed by the 1950 Indo-Sikkim Treaty, under which India controlled Sikkim's defence, external affairs, and communications — mirroring IoA subjects but through a different treaty mechanism. This treaty relationship distinguished Sikkim legally from all other acceding states.

**Causal relationship:** R correctly explains A. Because Sikkim was a protectorate under the 1950 Treaty rather than a paramountcy-era princely state, the IoA framework — which was designed for princely states — did not apply. Sikkim's integration required a fresh constitutional mechanism (the 36th Amendment).

Value Addition:
• The 1975 referendum in Sikkim resulted in over 97% voting for merger with India.
• China has historically not recognized Sikkim's merger as legitimate — it was only formally accepted by China in 2003.
• Article 2A, which added Sikkim to the First Schedule, was later deleted as a spent provision once Sikkim was fully integrated.

solution.concept_anchor: Voluntary accession vs. democratic legitimacy — UN Security Council debate
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because students who know India took the J&K case to the UN Security Council may assume India's position rested on legal formalism (the Maharaja's signature), when in fact the debate at the UN became more complex — involving both legalism and accusations of Pakistani aggression.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): The 'majority population determines accession' principle is Pakistan's argument, not India's — India relied on the ruler's signature as legally conclusive.
Eliminate option (d): 'Geographic contiguity supersedes all other considerations' was part of India's argument regarding Junagadh, not a universal principle India applied to J&K.

Eliminate option (a): While India did invoke legal formalism, the deeper tension at the UN was between the ruler's legal right to sign versus the population's democratic right to determine accession — the scenario asks for the 'core tension' this debate illustrates.

Retain option (c): The scenario illustrates the unresolved tension between legal formalism (ruler's signature as conclusive) and democratic legitimacy (plebiscite/popular will) — a tension that shaped India's international position and remains analytically central.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The reversed-causation trap targets students who assume legal formalism and democratic legitimacy are aligned in India's position. India's legal position (ruler's signature is conclusive) was reversed in causal direction by Pakistan's argument (popular will must override the ruler's decision). The scenario asks students to identify the unresolved theoretical tension — not which side 'won' at the UN — which requires understanding both positions without conflating them.
solution.final_explanation:
The J&K debate at the UN Security Council crystallized one of the deepest tensions in the IoA framework — between the letter of the law and democratic legitimacy.

**Applicable principle:** The IoA framework vested exclusive signing authority in the ruler. This made the instrument legally valid the moment the ruler signed it, regardless of popular opinion. However, democratic legitimacy principles — particularly the self-determination norm gaining traction post-1945 — argued that populations, not rulers, should determine accession.

**Why each option fails:**
• Option (a): 'Legal formalism always superseded popular will' overstates India's position — India itself used the plebiscite principle for Junagadh, showing it did not consistently hold this position.
• Option (b): 'Majority population determines accession' is Pakistan's — not India's — core legal argument.
• Option (d): Geographic contiguity was relevant to Junagadh but was never India's universal principle for J&K.
• Option (c): Correct. The core tension illustrated is between legal formalism (the ruler's signature under the IoA framework as legally conclusive) and democratic legitimacy (the argument that the people, not the ruler, should determine sovereign allegiance). This tension is unresolved in international law and defined India's conflicted position at the UN.

Value Addition:
• India's UN reference in January 1948 implicitly acknowledged the plebiscite commitment — later used against India.
• The UN Security Council passed Resolution 47 (1948) calling for a plebiscite in J&K — never implemented.
• Pakistan's argument exploited India's own use of the plebiscite principle in Junagadh — a documented legal inconsistency.

solution.concept_anchor: IoA — pre-constitutional statute, not Constitution-created
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is the primary trap — students who know Article 370 is the constitutional expression of J&K's accession may incorrectly conclude that the IoA itself was a creation of the Indian Constitution rather than a pre-constitutional British statute.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The Indian Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950 — years after most IoAs were signed (1947–1948). The IoA cannot be a creation of a document that did not exist when it was executed.
Eliminate option (b): Article 370 is the constitutional expression of J&K's restricted accession — it operationalizes the IoA's terms but did not create the IoA.
Eliminate option (c): The Government of India Act 1935 is not the statutory basis for the IoA — it governed British India's internal structure but not the IoA mechanism.
Retain option (d): Courts have consistently treated the IoA as a valid pre-constitutional instrument derived from the Indian Independence Act 1947 — not as a creature of the Indian Constitution.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits the confusion between what created the IoA (the Indian Independence Act 1947) and what gives it current constitutional relevance (Article 370 and related provisions). Students who know Article 370 is linked to the IoA may reverse the causal relationship — assuming the Constitution created the IoA — when in fact the IoA predates the Constitution and derives from a British statute. The Supreme Court has consistently upheld the IoA as a valid pre-constitutional instrument.
solution.final_explanation:
The IoA's legal character — as a pre-constitutional instrument — is foundational to understanding all judicial pronouncements about it.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: The Indian Constitution came into force on January 26, 1950. IoAs were signed between August 1947 and the late 1940s. A document signed years before the Constitution came into force cannot be a creation of that Constitution.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Article 370 operationalized J&K's restricted accession within the constitutional framework — it was the constitutional expression of the IoA's terms, not the source of the IoA's legal validity.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: The Government of India Act 1935 established British India's federal structure but did not create the IoA mechanism.
• Option (d) — Correct: Indian courts — from the Madhav Rao Scindia case (1971) to SBI v. Santosh Gupta (2017) — have consistently treated the IoA as a valid pre-constitutional instrument, legally grounded in the Indian Independence Act 1947. Its legal validity survived the transition from Dominion to Republic through the principle of continuity of legal obligations.

Value Addition:
• The IoA's legal continuity from the Dominion era to the Republic is an example of the general constitutional law principle that pre-constitutional obligations survive the enactment of a new constitution unless explicitly abrogated.
• No provision of the Indian Constitution explicitly 'validated' the IoA — courts inferred validity from the principle of legal continuity.
• This distinction is important for understanding why the IoA's abrogation (if ever held possible) would require more than a constitutional amendment.

solution.concept_anchor: Rulers who resisted accession to India — Bhopal, Travancore, Hyderabad
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) Travancore is deceptive because Travancore did initially declare independence under C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar — students who recall this may include it in the 'resistance' category along with Bhopal, Hyderabad, and Junagadh, missing that the question groups based on a different criterion.
elimination_logic: Bhopal's Nawab was the most reluctant and resistant ruler — clearly in the 'resistance' category.
Travancore declared independence initially — also a resistant state before reversing.
Hyderabad refused to accede and was the most extreme case of resistance — clearly fits.
Bikaner's Maharaja Ganga Singh was among the earliest and most enthusiastic supporters of accession to India — he was cooperative, not resistant.
Bikaner is the odd one out among rulers noted for resistance to accession. The answer is option (c).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap works by including Travancore as a distractor since students recall its initial independence declaration. Travancore did resist initially — making option (b) plausible. The key is that all three of Bhopal, Travancore, and Hyderabad can be characterized as resistant to accession in different degrees. Bikaner, by contrast, is documented as one of the most cooperative and willing states — Maharaja Ganga Singh was the first major ruler to publicly support accession to India, making it categorically different from the other three.
solution.final_explanation:
This question tests knowledge of which rulers resisted versus supported accession — a commonly tested distinction.

• Option (a) Bhopal — Not the odd one out: The Nawab of Bhopal was among the most persistent resisters — he engaged in prolonged negotiations, sought external support, and delayed signing until April 1949.
• Option (b) Travancore — Not the odd one out: C.P. Ramaswami Aiyar declared Travancore independent in June 1947, representing genuine initial resistance, before political pressure and an assassination attempt led to reversal.
• Option (c) Bikaner — Correct odd one out: Maharaja Ganga Singh of Bikaner was among the earliest and most enthusiastic supporters of accession to India. He signed promptly and publicly advocated for integration, serving as a counter-example to resistant rulers.
• Option (d) Hyderabad — Not the odd one out: The Nizam's resistance was the most extreme — lasting 14 months before military resolution.

Value Addition:
• Bikaner's cooperation was partly strategic — Ganga Singh recognized that Bikaner was surrounded by Indian territory and had little strategic depth for independence.
• The 'triangle of resistance' (Bhopal, Travancore, Hyderabad) is a useful mnemonic for UPSC purposes.
• Ganga Singh had also represented Indian princely states at the Paris Peace Conference (1919) — he was an internationally experienced ruler.

solution.concept_anchor: Article 370 — concurrence mechanism vs. IoA three-subject limit

statement_analysis.statement: Under Article 370, Parliament's legislative power for J&K was initially confined to Defence, External Affairs, and Communications — the same three subjects specified in J&K's Instrument of Accession.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 370 gave constitutional form to J&K's restricted accession. Parliament's initial legislative competence for J&K mirrored the IoA's three-subject limitation. Extension to other subjects required a separate procedure under Article 370(1).

statement_analysis.statement: For subjects beyond the three IoA subjects, Parliament could extend its legislative authority to J&K through a Presidential Order issued after obtaining the concurrence of the J&K government — a requirement that applied equally to both the Union List and the Concurrent List.
statement_analysis.reason: Article 370(1)(b) and (d) provided that for matters beyond the IoA subjects, Presidential Orders could extend Union or Concurrent List subjects to J&K with the concurrence of J&K's government — this applied to both lists, making the concurrence requirement uniform across Union and Concurrent List extensions.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) is deceptive because students who know Statement 1 is correct may not be certain about Statement 2's precision on whether the concurrence requirement applies equally to both lists — and may assume only one list required concurrence.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Parliament's initial legislative competence for J&K was limited to the IoA's three subjects under Article 370 — this is accurate. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2: The concurrence of J&K's government was required for extending both Union List and Concurrent List subjects to J&K beyond the IoA subjects. Article 370(1)(b) covered Union List extensions; Article 370(1)(d) covered other matters including Concurrent List — both required concurrence. Statement 2 is correct.
Both statements correct → option (a).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 is a scope-extension test: students who know concurrence was required for some extensions but are uncertain whether it applied 'equally' to both lists may reject Statement 2 as an over-claim. The key is that Article 370's concurrence mechanism did apply to both Union and Concurrent List extensions beyond the IoA subjects — the requirement was uniform. Students who recall only the Concurrent List concurrence requirement (the more commonly cited example) may doubt the Union List application.
solution.final_explanation:
Article 370 created a constitutional architecture that precisely mirrored the IoA's limited scope while providing a mechanism for gradual expansion.

• Statement 1 — Correct: J&K's IoA covered only Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. Article 370 gave this restriction constitutional form — Parliament's legislative authority for J&K began with only these subjects, directly mirroring the IoA's scope.
• Statement 2 — Correct: Article 370(1)(b) provided that Parliament could legislate on Union List matters (beyond the IoA subjects) for J&K via Presidential Order with J&K government's concurrence. Article 370(1)(d) extended this to other constitutional provisions including Concurrent List matters. The concurrence requirement was consistently applied to both lists — distinguishing J&K's constitutional relationship from that of all other states.

Value Addition:
• Over time (1947–1994), virtually all Union and Concurrent List subjects were extended to J&K through Presidential Orders — making Article 370 progressively less distinctive in practice.
• The 2019 Presidential Order used the J&K Legislative Assembly (under President's Rule) as the equivalent of the J&K government for concurrence purposes.
• After the 2023 Supreme Court judgment, Article 370's abrogation stands as constitutionally valid — though the IoA's underlying legal status as a historical document is separate.

solution.concept_anchor: Hyderabad's unique legal pathway — multiple distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: Unlike most other princely states, Hyderabad's Standstill Agreement with India was signed after the lapse of British paramountcy — making it the only state that negotiated both the Standstill and the lapse as a technically independent sovereign.
statement_analysis.reason: Hyderabad's Standstill Agreement was signed in November 1947 — after the paramountcy lapse of August 15, 1947. This means Hyderabad negotiated as a technically independent entity (post-paramountcy lapse) rather than as a state still under paramountcy — a unique legal feature of its transition.

statement_analysis.statement: Hyderabad's Nizam filed a formal complaint before the United Nations Security Council against India's military action in September 1948.
statement_analysis.reason: The Nizam did file a complaint with the UN Security Council following Operation Polo. The complaint was not pursued further after Hyderabad's integration was completed and the Nizam accepted the post-integration reality.

statement_analysis.statement: Hyderabad's post-integration Merger Agreement of 1948 was legally equivalent to an Instrument of Accession and served the same constitutional function.
statement_analysis.reason: The Merger Agreement and the IoA were legally distinct instruments. The IoA was a voluntary sovereignty transfer on specific subjects; the Merger Agreement was a post-conquest constitutional formality acknowledging the new political reality. They served different legal functions and arose from different circumstances.

statement_analysis.statement: Hyderabad remained under Indian military administration (as a 'Governor's Province') for approximately one year after Operation Polo before a civilian government was installed.
statement_analysis.reason: Hyderabad was placed under Military Governor (Major General J.N. Chaudhuri) immediately after Operation Polo, but it was designated as a 'Military Governorate' — not a Governor's Province in the constitutional sense. Moreover, civilian administration was restored in relatively short order, not stretched over a full year in the manner suggested.

solution.strong_distractor: c — Option (c) 'Only three' is deceptive because students who correctly verify Statements 1 and 2 and then hastily accept Statement 3 (which sounds legally plausible) will over-count.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Hyderabad's Standstill was signed post-paramountcy lapse (November 1947) — it did negotiate as a technically independent entity. Correct.
Statement 2: The Nizam did file a UN complaint — historically documented. Correct.
Statement 3: Claims Merger Agreement was 'legally equivalent' to IoA — this is the partial-truth trap; they are legally distinct instruments. Incorrect.
Statement 4: 'Governor's Province' and 'approximately one year' are imprecise characterizations — Hyderabad was a Military Governorate and civilian restoration was faster. Incorrect.
Only Statements 1 and 2 correct → 'Only two' → option (b).
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 3 is the partial-truth trap: students who know a 'Merger Agreement' existed for Hyderabad post-integration may accept that it 'served the same constitutional function' as an IoA — because both are integration instruments. The crucial distinction is that an IoA is a voluntary sovereignty transfer; the Merger Agreement was a post-conquest formality. Equating them conflates legal instruments that arose from entirely different circumstances and carried different legal implications.
solution.final_explanation:
Hyderabad's integration has multiple distinctive legal features — students must verify each claim precisely.

• Statement 1 — Correct: All other states that signed Standstill Agreements did so while still under paramountcy (pre-August 15, 1947) or immediately around its lapse. Hyderabad's Standstill was signed in November 1947 — after paramountcy had lapsed — making the Nizam technically an independent sovereign during the negotiation.
• Statement 2 — Correct: The Nizam filed a complaint with the UN Security Council in September 1948 after Operation Polo. This is a documented historical fact, though the complaint was withdrawn/not pursued after integration was complete.
• Statement 3 — Incorrect: The Merger Agreement and the IoA are not legally equivalent. The IoA was a voluntary pre-military transfer of sovereignty on three subjects. The Merger Agreement was a constitutional formality executed after military conquest — its legal character was entirely different.
• Statement 4 — Incorrect: Hyderabad was placed under a 'Military Governorate' (with J.N. Chaudhuri as Military Governor), not a 'Governor's Province.' The characterization of 'approximately one year' for the military administration period overstates its duration.

Value Addition:
• J.N. Chaudhuri (later COAS) served as Hyderabad's Military Governor after Operation Polo.
• Hyderabad's state was reorganized and its territory distributed among Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka after the States Reorganisation Act 1956.
• The Nizam's personal wealth made him one of the world's richest individuals — his negotiation was also partly about preserving his personal assets.

solution.concept_anchor: Kalat accession to Pakistan — parallel to J&K for India
solution.strong_distractor: a — Option (a) is deceptive because Bahawalpur's accession to Pakistan is the most commonly cited example of a Pakistan-side IoA, and students who know it existed may not know whether it was disputed or cooperative — confusing it with Kalat's disputed case.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (b): Junagadh acceded to Pakistan — but Junagadh's accession is associated with the Hindu-majority population dispute, not a dispute parallel to J&K on the Pakistan side.
Eliminate option (d): Khairpur acceded to Pakistan through a cooperative, undisputed IoA — it is not the Pakistani parallel to J&K.
Eliminate option (a): Bahawalpur's accession to Pakistan was cooperative and undisputed — it is the 'Mysore of Pakistan's accessions,' not the disputed parallel.

Retain option (c): Kalat's accession to Pakistan (1948) is the closest parallel to J&K's disputed accession to India — the Khan of Kalat initially claimed independence after paramountcy lapse and disputed accession conditions, creating a sovereignty controversy that mirrors the J&K situation on the Pakistan side.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The conflation trap merges 'Pakistan-side accession' with 'disputed accession' — students who know Bahawalpur and Khairpur are often-cited Pakistan accessions may conflate them with the disputed case. Kalat is the specifically disputed case — the Khan initially claimed Kalat was fully independent (like Hyderabad's claim), and his brother led an insurgency against accession. This mirrors J&K's disputed accession to India, making Kalat the analytically relevant parallel.
solution.final_explanation:
The IoA framework was symmetrical — both Dominions received accessions, and both had disputed cases that generated lasting political controversies.

• Option (a) Bahawalpur — Incorrect: Bahawalpur's Nawab signed the IoA to Pakistan promptly and cooperatively. It is the Pakistani equivalent of Mysore — a cooperative, undisputed accession.
• Option (b) Junagadh — Incorrect: Junagadh's IoA to Pakistan is relevant to the India-Pakistan dispute from India's side — it is not the Pakistani parallel to J&K. Junagadh's dispute arose because India challenged its validity.
• Option (c) Kalat — Correct: Kalat is the closest Pakistan-side parallel to J&K. The Khan of Kalat claimed independence after the paramountcy lapse (arguing Kalat had a different relationship with the British than ordinary princely states). He eventually signed an IoA under pressure. His brother Ahmad Yar Khan led an insurgency, and the sovereignty dispute over Kalat has echoes to this day — making it the analytically correct pair.
• Option (d) Khairpur — Incorrect: Khairpur's accession to Pakistan was cooperative and undisputed — it does not present analytical parallels to J&K's contested accession.

Value Addition:
• The Balochistan insurgency in Pakistan has historical roots partly in the disputed Kalat accession.
• The Khan of Kalat argued that Kalat had treaty relationships with the British Crown that were different in character from ordinary paramountcy — paralleling J&K's claim to special status.
• Understanding the symmetry of the IoA framework helps answer questions about why both India and Pakistan have contested accession cases.

solution.concept_anchor: IoA template clauses — Clause 7 and Clause 8 distinctions

statement_analysis.statement: The 'no prejudice' clause (Clause 7) of the standardized IoA template meant that accession did not automatically commit rulers to joining any future Indian constitution — a separate political process was required for full constitutional integration.
statement_analysis.reason: Clause 7 explicitly protected rulers from being automatically bound by any future constitution India might adopt. This is why full constitutional integration required separate Merger Agreements and, in J&K's case, a distinct constitutional mechanism (Article 370).

statement_analysis.statement: The schedule appended to each IoA listed the specific subjects on which Parliament could legislate for that acceding state, and this schedule could include any number of subjects from the Union List at the ruler's discretion.
statement_analysis.reason: The schedule was standardized and limited to the three subjects of Defence, External Affairs, and Communications. Rulers could not add additional subjects from the Union List at their discretion — the IoA template was uniform on this point. Additional subjects required separate legal instruments.

statement_analysis.statement: Clause 8 of the IoA template preserved the ruler's authority over all matters not specified in the accession schedule — this residual sovereignty was the legal basis for rulers' resistance to full administrative absorption.
statement_analysis.reason: Clause 8's residual sovereignty protection meant rulers retained governance authority over everything outside the three acceded subjects. This is why separate Merger Agreements (with privy purse as consideration) were needed to achieve full administrative absorption — the IoA alone was legally insufficient for that purpose.

solution.strong_distractor: d — Option (d) listing all three as correct is deceptive because Statements 1 and 3 are both accurate and well-reasoned, creating pressure to accept Statement 2 as correct without careful analysis.
elimination_logic: Statement 1: Clause 7's 'no prejudice' protection against automatic constitutional commitment — accurate and well-documented. Statement 1 is correct.

Statement 2 claims rulers could include 'any number of subjects from the Union List at their discretion' — this is a scope-extension; the template was standardized at three subjects, not customizable. Statement 2 is incorrect.
Statement 3: Clause 8 residual sovereignty as the legal basis for resistance to full absorption — accurate. Statement 3 is correct.
Statements 1 and 3 correct, Statement 2 incorrect → option (c): 1 and 3 only.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Statement 2 uses 'at the ruler's discretion' — a scope-extension that sounds plausible because rulers did negotiate IoA terms and the template was presented as something rulers could 'accept.' However, the subject coverage was non-negotiable: the template uniformly limited legislative coverage to three subjects. Students who know rulers had some negotiating room (on privy purse amounts, succession rights, etc.) may incorrectly assume this extended to the IoA's subject coverage.
solution.final_explanation:
The IoA template's specific clauses defined both what was transferred and what was retained — each clause had a distinct legal function.

• Statement 1 — Correct: Clause 7 is among the most legally significant clauses in the IoA. It protected rulers from being automatically swept into any future constitution India adopted. This clause is the direct legal ancestor of the 'separate constitutional mechanism' requirement — exemplified by Article 370 for J&K and merger covenants for other states.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect: The schedule was standardized, not customizable. It covered Defence, External Affairs, and Communications only. The uniformity of the schedule was essential to V.P. Menon's strategy — it prevented rulers from demanding individual carve-outs for specific subjects, which would have made negotiations interminable.
• Statement 3 — Correct: Clause 8 gave rulers legal standing to resist full administrative takeover — they had a valid legal basis for retaining governance authority over non-acceded subjects. Merger Agreements needed to provide sufficient consideration (privy purse, personal privileges) to overcome this legal protection.

Value Addition:
• The 'no prejudice' clause (Clause 7) is why J&K's ruler could legitimately argue for special terms when the Indian Constitution was being drafted.
• V.P. Menon's standardization of the schedule (three subjects only) was a deliberate strategy to get quick signatures — reducing the instrument's scope made it less threatening to rulers.
• Clause 8's residual sovereignty protection lapsed upon signing a Merger Agreement — rulers gave it up in exchange for privy purses.

• Rajasthan's seven-stage formation (1948–1950) is one of the most studied examples of collective covenant integration.
• PEPSU was eventually merged into Punjab by the States Reorganisation Act 1956 on linguistic grounds.

elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): The scenario involves a ruler's voluntary signature on a sovereignty document — not a merger after military action. Military-forced integration (Hyderabad model) would not involve a voluntary IoA.
Eliminate option (b): The Constitution operationalized accession terms but was not itself the source of the IoA's legal validity — the Indian Independence Act 1947 is the primary statutory source.

Eliminate option (d): International customary law on self-determination is relevant but is Pakistan's argument, not India's legal basis for the IoA — and it does not explain the ruler's authority to sign.

Retain option (c): The scenario involves a ruler voluntarily signing a sovereignty document under a British statute (Indian Independence Act 1947) — the IoA is a pre-constitutional voluntary instrument whose legal validity rests on this statute, as upheld by Indian courts.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: Option (b) is the partial-truth trap: the Constitution does incorporate accession-related provisions (Articles 1, 370, etc.) and courts have upheld accession commitments within the constitutional framework. Students who know this constitutional relevance may overlook the pre-constitutional statutory origin — the Indian Independence Act 1947 — which is the primary legal source. The Constitution built upon the IoA; it did not create it.
solution.final_explanation:
This scenario tests the ability to identify the correct legal principle governing a ruler's voluntary accession under a British statute.

**Applicable principle:** The IoA was a pre-constitutional instrument deriving its authority from the Indian Independence Act 1947. When a ruler voluntarily signed the IoA, the legal basis for that signature — and its binding effect — was the 1947 Act, not any subsequent Indian constitutional provision. Courts have consistently upheld this analysis.

**Why each option fails:**
• Option (a): Military-forced integration was the Hyderabad model — no formal IoA was signed in that scenario. The present scenario involves voluntary signature.
• Option (b): The Constitution operationalized accession terms but was not itself the source of the IoA's legal validity. The Indian Independence Act 1947 is the primary statutory authority.
• Option (c): Correct. The scenario describes a voluntary sovereignty transfer by a ruling prince under a pre-constitutional British statute (the Indian Independence Act 1947). The legal principle is that the IoA was a valid pre-constitutional instrument whose legal force survived the transition from Dominion to Republic — upheld in Madhav Rao Scindia (1971) and SBI v. Santosh Gupta (2017).
• Option (d): International customary law on self-determination is the opposing argument — it does not explain the legal basis for the ruler's authority to sign the IoA within the domestic Indian legal framework.

Value Addition:
• The continuity of legal obligations across the Dominion-Republic transition is a foundational principle of Indian constitutional law.
• Pakistan tried to argue at the UN that IoA-based accessions violated self-determination — but Indian courts applied domestic legal standards, not international customary law.
• The IoA's pre-constitutional nature explains why abrogating Article 370 did not require amending the IoA itself.

Students who know geography was central to India's case may accept 'Junagadh shared a border with Pakistan' as India's argument without catching that it is the opposite — India argued Junagadh was NOT contiguous with Pakistan. The word 'appropriate' in the statement combined with the correct geographic concept creates a superficially convincing but factually reversed claim.
solution.final_explanation:
Junagadh's accession case tests precise knowledge of India's legal arguments — including their geographical dimension.

• Statement 1 — Correct (not the 'incorrect' statement): The Nawab's legal authority was indeed exclusive under the IoA framework — rulers could accede to either Dominion. Pakistan's legal position was entirely consistent with the IoA's design. India disputed the practical validity on other grounds.
• Statement 2 — Incorrect (the NOT correct statement): India's geographic argument was that Junagadh was NOT contiguous with Pakistan — entirely surrounded by Indian territory and the Arabian Sea, making Pakistan-accession geographically anomalous. The statement incorrectly claims India argued Junagadh 'shared a border with Pakistan' — reversing the actual argument.
• Statement 3 — Correct (not the 'incorrect' statement): After the Nawab fled to Karachi in November 1947, India took administrative control and organized a plebiscite in February 1948. • The Nawab's successor (as a Pakistani citizen) filed cases in Indian courts claiming Junagadh's territory — these cases continued for decades.
• The Gir Forest (home to Asiatic Lions) is located within what was formerly Junagadh state.

solution.concept_anchor: Section 7 — paramountcy lapse, not transfer
solution.strong_distractor: b — Option (b) is deceptive because students know Section 6 of the Indian Independence Act is important for accession and may confuse it with Section 7, which deals specifically with the paramountcy lapse.
elimination_logic: Eliminate option (a): Section 5 dealt with the Governor-General's powers — not paramountcy.
Eliminate option (b): Section 6 enabled Dominion Parliament legislation to extend to acceding states — important for accession mechanics but not the paramountcy lapse provision.
Eliminate option (c): Section 8 dealt with the Governor-General's suzerainty duties — not the primary paramountcy lapse provision.

Retain option (d): Section 7 of the Indian Independence Act 1947 specifically provided that His Majesty's sovereignty over the Indian states would lapse — paramountcy ended by this section, not transferred.
solution.upsc_trap_explanation: The entity-swap trap exploits knowledge of the Indian Independence Act's provisions. Students who know Section 6 is the key accession provision may swap it with Section 7 (the paramountcy lapse provision) — both are critical but distinct. Section 6 enabled Dominion legislation to extend to acceding states; Section 7 ended paramountcy. The two sections are frequently confused in examination contexts.
solution.final_explanation:
The Indian Independence Act 1947 contained multiple critical provisions for the IoA framework — Section 6 and Section 7 are distinct and must not be confused.

• Option (a) — Incorrect: Section 5 of the Indian Independence Act dealt with the Governor-General's powers during the transition — not paramountcy arrangements.
• Option (b) — Incorrect: Section 6 is the accession-enabling provision — it allowed Dominion legislation to apply to acceding states and gave legal effect to IoAs. It did not address the lapse of paramountcy.
• Option (c) — Incorrect: Section 8 addressed the Governor-General's obligations regarding existing treaties and arrangements — not the termination of paramountcy.
• Option (d) — Correct: Section 7 provided that from August 15, 1947, His Majesty's sovereignty over Indian states — exercised through paramountcy — would lapse. It explicitly stated paramountcy could not be transferred to either Dominion. This section is the statutory basis for princes' temporary independence and their theoretical freedom not to accede.

Value Addition:
• Section 6 (accession enabling) and Section 7 (paramountcy lapse) together created the IoA framework — both must be read together for a complete understanding.
• The phrase 'paramountcy shall lapse' in Section 7 is among the most consequential in Indian legal history.
• The deliberate non-transfer of paramountcy to either Dominion was a British decision to avoid creating a new imperial successor — states were to be free to choose.
